Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
Greetings

It was recently noted by a poster (sk...@columbia.edu) that some of the 7
original clan hoser cards have been altered between the Jyhad and V:tES
editions.

These cards (one for each Camarilla clan) are: Brujah Frenzy, Gangrel
De-evolution, Malkavian Dementia, Nosferatu Putrescence, Letter from
Vienna, Tragic Love Affair, and Cultivated Blood Shortage. Gangrel
De-Evolution was renamed Gangrel Atavism for the V:tES set.

In the original set, none of these had any clan requirements. Since their
purpose was to hose a particular clan, they were only usable is someone
*else* was playing that clan. Within the game design, they serves as a
safeguard in case some particular clan should turn out to be too powerful.
That did in fact turn out to be the case for Malkavian Dementia, which was
often used to counteract the power and popularity of Malkavian S&B. Most
of the other clan hosers are rarely used. They hardly needed additional
restrictions, espectially since the current number of clans (21) makes it
far harder to predict what clans one's opponent will be playing.

I have none of the V:tES versions of these cards so I checked out the
on-line WOTC card-text listings. Three cards have apparently been
changed: Gangrel Atavism now requires you control a ready Gangrel, Tragic
Love Affair now requires a ready Toreador, and Brujah Frenzy now requires
you control a ready Brujah.

Could find no errata among the current listings. Why were the cards
changed? Are the V:tES versions now official?

Since Gangrel Atavism and Gangrel De-Evolution differ in more than
name (like Stake and Wooden Stake), should they now be treated as two
separate cards?

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Lupus Australius wrote:
"That did in fact turn out to be the case for Malkavian Dementia, which was
often used to counteract the power and popularity of Malkavian S&B. Most of
the other clan hosers are rarely used. They hardly needed additional
restrictions, espectially since the current number of clans (21) makes it far
harder to predict what clans one's opponent will be playing."

Just as an aside, Clan hosers are complely unneeded in the game, and are pretty
much contrary to the entire original design paradigm of the game. The bulk of
Jyhad was designed to exist without the need of "Hoser Cards", and plays just
fine without them. The Malkavian Dementia that is used for an example is
completely unneeded to defend against the Malkavians, as any number of standard
defenses/strategies (Rush combat/Bleed Bounce/Out race them) work just fine.
The Clan Hosers were sort of a goofy idea that was an attempt to get some game
world flavor into the set, but were more a left over from the M:TG game
mechanic than a part of the Jyhad game mechanic.

As a balancing factor, they are very sketchy. Malkavian Dementia (again, for
instance, as it pretty much is the most effective of the clan hosers) is only
useful if A) there is a Malkavian sitting next to you and B) You draw it. For
there to be a Malkavian to be sitting next to you, you need to be either really
lucky or know before hand that there are Malkavians playing. To know there are
Malkavians playing, you need to either spy on your opponents and then change
your deck in response (like Sideboarding or something), which is really lame,
or be playing in your standard playgroup and picking on the guy who always
plays Malkavians, which is also lame. To be able to draw the hoser card, you
will need multiples of them in your deck to count as a viable defense. Having
alot of them will hamstring your deck against anything but a Malkavian, and
having few will just get you killed if you are relying on it as your defense.

All in all, the clan hosers are a bad idea from a design standpoint and a bad
idea from a strategy standpoint. I'd just stay away from them.

(if you haven't already read the response from LSJ, the Clan requirment symbols
on the VTES versions of these cards, as well as the lack of them from a couple
others like Asylum Hunting ground, is a misprint. You don't need a Malkavian
to play Malk Dementia.)

There is no debate as to whether or not they exist nor whether or not they
should exist, just whether they are either useful or balanced. I would claim
that they are an example of bad game design because depending on the situation
they are either completely useless or overly powerful and as a result, not
particularly balanced (the Malk Dementia is probably the only one that fits
this bill, as game effects that pretty much allow you to burn an opponents
vampire are very few and far between, and generally have a pretty severe cost.
The only cost of Malk Dementia is that of opportunity) .

Granted, most of the basic set Clan Hoser cards pretty much suck, but here they
are:

Malkavian Dementia--Far and away the best of the lot. Very useful for killing
off Malkavians ("Oh no! Zebulon has deablerized Gilbert Duane! He is outraged
at his own actions and calls a blood hunt! Oh, the Inhumanity!"). The need
for the Malkavian to be untapped is kind of a hamstring, but isn't a problem if
you get it in your hand in the first 4 or 5 turns (when vampires are coming
under control) or if there is something to sack vampires to (like Antedeluvian
Awakening or Golconda).

Brujah Frenzy--Possibly effective, as it will save one of your vampires from a
Bum's Rush, but that is pretty much it, as it is unlikely that neither the
Brujah or the frenzy victim will actually want to fight.

Letter from Vienna--Sketchy, at best. Ok, it taps all the Tremere, but if the
Tremere are untapped waiting to intercept/bleed bounce you, then they most
likely are packing WWEF, making the Letter useless, and if they can't
intercept/bounce you anyway, what difference does it make if they are tapped or
not?

Cultivated Blood Shortage--Could be slightly effective, except that it has a +1
stealth built in destruction clause. At best, it will make the Ventrue player
waste a few actions killing it.

Gangrel Atavism--Blows. Darn! My Gangrel has -1 bleed? I guess I'll just
have to kill you instead...

Tragic Love Affair--Somewhat debilitating for the one turn that it will be
around, as it is really easy to get rid of, either by placing it on another
Toreador or by ditching the edge.

Nosferatu Putrescence--Very far from useful. The -1 hand damage that it gives
out is only useful in multiples, and having multiples of this card is idiocy.

Out of all of them, the only one that is particularly debilitating is the
Malkavian Dementia, as more often than not, its use will result in one (if not
two) destroyed Malkavians. The rest are merely nuisance. As such, the set of
them are mostly not worth even putting in your deck when playing blind (as even
with a 90 card deck, card space is at a premium most of the time), and putting
them in your deck because you know what your opponent is playing is (in gamer
terms) ethically questionable (the DCI Jyhad tournament rules do not utilize
any sort of "sideboarding", as Jyhad is designed to be played on the strength
of deck design, not hoser inclusion).

The newer set inclusions in the Clan Hoser world are pretty wack as well. Most
of them are little more than minor inconvinience (Giovanni Discrimination,
Whispers of the Niktuku) and some of them are completely unacceptable (Out of
Control comes to mind...). Malkavian Derangement, when compared to Malk
Dementia, is far more balanced (costs 2 pool and requires a coin flip offset by
lack of opportunity cost), and as a result much less effective.

fun, even if you are not trying to "hose" the Malkavian player. First
off, there were only 7 clans (not counting caitiff) in the original design
of the game. Imagine a 5 player game, in which each player has 3 or 4
vampires out (total of 12-16 vampires, not counting your own). The odds
are pretty good (in the original 7-clan setup) that at least one of those
vampires is going to be a Malkavian. If you can get them untapped, they
can be used for free actions. Even if tapped, they can be used for votes,
or to block with WWEF.

> All in all, the clan hosers are a bad idea from a design standpoint and a bad
> idea from a strategy standpoint. I'd just stay away from them.

Well, I would today, with 20 clans in the game. In such an environment,
cards that target specific clans need to have a more general usefulness as
well. I would not put Malkavian Dementia in one of my decks today,
as I would probably find myself facing Malkavian Antitribu, instead.

"Seeds of Corruption" comes to mind, as, while it is particularly
useful against Settites, it is still useful even if none are on the table.

Lupus Australius wrote:
"Meaning what? In a CCG game, additional cards and new expansions are there to
add variety and possibilities. Very few cards can be said to be "needed" in
any absolute sense. If a card is "needed" then that is generally taken as a
sign that card is overpowered and the game is unbalanced."

Yes, yes, semantics are wonderful. Cards that fit into a game do so because
they are compatable with the game design and add something to the game as a
whole. Clan Hosers in Jyhad, IMO, are poorly compatable with the game design
as a whole. Yes, they were in the basic set, but were a bad idea then. Jyhad
stands as a very good example of a game where good deck design and good
strategy are of a paramount importance. Hoser cards (single cards that shut
down entire strategies but are completely useless in most situations) do not
add to this sort of enviornment.

"How can you defend such a statement when the "clan hosers" *were* in fact part
of the original design, for good or ill."

Just because they were in the main set doesn't mean they were a good idea. I
understand that they were included as a representation of the various clans
disadvantages, but when compared to the rest of the set, they stand out as an
odd inclusion.

"You could say the same for any other 7 cards in the game. In fact, one could
argue that the game plays just fine without any of the expansions."

Well no, you couldn't. Most of the cards in the game are general purpose cards
to build strategies around. The Clan Hosers are incredibly specialized and
mostly useless, unless you know what clans your opponents are playing. Most
other card in the set (barring a few weak exceptions. Most specific anti-vote
cards come to mind) are useful in any situation and, depending on your
strategy, always worth including in your deck. Specific hoser cards do not fit
this description.

"It is useful against Malkavians, so who cares whether it is "needed"."

So are many other non specific strategies that do not rely on either luckily
being next to a Malkavian or knowning before you play that you will.

"I can remember a time when posters on this ng were lamenting the power of
Malkavians, and saying "Thank God for Malkavian Dementia""

Yes. Because they didn't really understand the game (myself included).

"I don't think you get this card at all. It can be quite useful, and also fun,
even if you are not trying to "hose" the Malkavian player."

No, I understand the card perfectly. I play it on your untapped Malkavian, use
him to diablerize your other torporized Malkavian, and call a blood hunt on the
first Malkavian. You now have had 2 vampires burned with very little
effort/cost on my part. This is pretty much what has happened every single
time I have played Malkavian Dementia.

""Seeds of Corruption" comes to mind, as, while it is particularly
useful against Settites, it is still useful even if none are on the table."

Exactly. Seeds of Corruption is a perfectly acceptable card, as it is not
highly situational. The Clan Hosers as a whole are incedibly sketchy, as
again, they are not worth including in your deck unless you know you will be
playing against a certain clan, and if you put them in your deck because you
know you are going to be playing against said clan, you are gaining an unfair
advantage.

20-20 foresight in such matters. In this light, grandiose statements like
the one above sound pompous and arrogant. Only hindsight (and the
specific game environment you play in) will tell if certain cards "are
compatible" with the "game design".

Many clan hosers did not in fact turn out to be wallpaper, at least not in
a 7-clan multi-player environment. You have complained, in fact, that
Malkavian Dementia can be too effective. Malkavian Dementia is "too
effective" only a player is too predictable and has no sense of humor. It

set, and certainly never stopped them from winning more than their fair
share of games and tournaments.

> where good deck design and good strategy are of a paramount importance.

Lets not leave out variety, originality, unpredictability, atmosphere, and
fun.

> Hoser cards (single cards that shut down entire strategies but are
> completely useless in most situations) do not add to this sort of
> enviornment.

environment where I knew what my opponents were playing. I felt they
added variety, unpredictability, and fun to the decks. I did not use them
to hose particular strategies, or shut down entire decks. If I was
playing a Nosferatu vote deck, I might include Cultivated Blood Shortage
to cause some trouble for any Ventrue, because they were the clan most
likely to cause me trouble with vote competition. One or two Malkavian
Dementias was often a good idea in a 4 or 5 player game (and we
sometimes even played 9 player games), because one could use them to
perform extra actions, gain extra votes, temporarily deprive an opponent
of a minion, etc, etc. Brujah Frenzy was also a fun "surprise" card in a
multi-player setup, though not as effective or likely to be used, since
the Brujah were considerably less popular than the Malkavians. One such
card in a deck was for fun and unpredictablility, and if the clan in
question was not being played, it could be easily discarded.

> "How can you defend such a statement when the "clan hosers" *were* in
> fact part of the original design, for good or ill."

> Just because they were in the main set doesn't mean they were a good
> idea. I understand that they were included as a representation of the
> various clans disadvantages, but when compared to the rest of the set,
> they stand out as an odd inclusion.

They are not much different from:

Ancestor's Talisman: Only useful if an opponent plays action cards
requiring Dominate or Presence.

Kindred Segregation; Sacre-Cour Cathedral; Wave of Insanity; Command;
Eyes of the Serpent; Art of Love; Coagulate Blood: Only useful if an
opponent is plays with Allies.

Far Mastery; Lure of the Serpent: Only usable if an opponent plays allies
or retainers.

Shepherd's Innocence: Only usable if one of your opponent plays
permanents requiring animalism

Peace Treaty; Up Yours; Fast Hands: Only useful if your opponent relies
on weapons.

Blessing of Durga Syn; Shattering Blow; Fractured Armament: Only usable
if an opponent plays equipment.

Ancilla Empowerment: Only useful if your opponent plays weenie decks.

Arcanum Chapterhouse Alexandria: Only useful if predator or prey play
Hunting Grounds Cards.

Archon Investigation: Only usable if your predator likes to bleed for 4+.

Justicar Retribution: Only useful if an opponent uses permanent bleed
enhancers or IC members.

Protected Resources: Only useful if an opponent bleeds for 3+.

Anachronism: Only usable if an opponent plays big vampires with weapons.

Betrayer: Only usable if your opponent is has the same vampires in play
as you do in your uncontrolled region.

Dog Pack: Only useful if an apponent plays combat-ends strike cards.

Beyond Reproach: Only useful if your opponent plays Primogen.

Command of the Harpies; The Treatment: Only useful if your opponent plays
Princes.

Wrath of the Inner Circle: Only useful if your opponent plays Justicars.

Fear of Mekhet: Only usable if an opponent plays Justicars of IC Members.

Open Grate: Only usable if an opponent plays press cards.

Disputed Territory; Arson; Rampage; Unnatural Disaster; etc: Only useful
if your opponent uses Locations.

Mark of the Damned: Only useful if your prey likes to burn his prey's
vampires.

The Portrait, The Signet of King Saul, Legacy of Caine: Only useful if
your prey plays big vampires.

Rotschreck: Only usable if an opponent plays aggravated damage.

Sacrifice; Clan Loyalty: Only usable if someone else is playing the same
clan as you are.

Weakness: Only usable if an opponent plays Master: Discipline cards.

Any reaction card that is "only usable during a political action":
Pointless unless an opponent plays political actions.

Night Moves; Forgotten Labyrinth; (or any card that gives more than +1
stealth): Pointless unless your opponent plays intercept.

Then we have some of the new Anti-Sect cards. These are a similar concept
to the Anti-Clan cards, but more viable because there are only 3 sects,
while there were originally 8 clans (Now 22). MtG has 5 factions, which
is one reason why faction hosers work better in Magic than clan-hosers do
in Jyhad.

Covenant of Blood: Only usable if your opponent plays Camarilla vampires.

Imperial Decree; Judgement-Camarilla Segregation: Only useful if an
opponent plays non-camarilla vampires.

Monomancy; Vaulderie: Only usable if an opponent plays Sabbat vampires.

The above list is by no means complete. All of the cards listed above are
cards whose usefulness or usability are dependent on what one's opponent
has in his deck. Any deck designer takes into account his game
environment when he designes his deck. If one's opponents have lots of
intercept, you need lots of stealth. If lots of bleed decks you need
bleed defence, if lots of vote decks you need vote defence, if lots of
combat decks you need combat defence, etc. etc. One can never be
predictable in what decks one plays because there is no deck so good that
it cannot be countered.

The clan hosers listed above are in no way out of spirit with the game,
and are no different in spirit than many of the cards listed above. I
accept that they are too specific to be often useful (far more so now than
they used to be, due to the proliferation of the number of clans), and
this can be attributed to a certain shortsightedness in design. So what?
Many cards have turned out to be wallpaper and this is inevitable in any
deck design. Everyone has 20/20 hindsight. However, if I was playing in
a game environment where I were constantly being hosed by Brujah rush
decks, I might well put a Brujah Frenzy of two in my next deck. Why not?

> "You could say the same for any other 7 cards in the game. In fact, one
> could argue that the game plays just fine without any of the
> expansions."

> Well no, you couldn't.

Well, yes you could. In case you forgot, this was in reference to your
statement that "the game plays just fine without them". Please name seven
cards, and explain how their absence would make Jyhad unplayable.

> Most of the cards in the game are general
> purpose cards to build strategies around. The Clan Hosers are
> incredibly specialized and mostly useless, unless you know what clans
> your opponents are playing. Most other card in the set (barring a few
> weak exceptions. Most specific anti-vote cards come to mind) are useful
> in any situation and, depending on your strategy, always worth including
> in your deck. Specific hoser cards do not fit this description.

Neither do the "weak exceptions", a significant number of which are listed
above, and some of which are not so weak. As I have shown, there are a
significant number of these in Jyhad. While they may be rarely played,
they do serve as a deterrent to predictability in the decks one plays. If
you are too predictable, they WILL be used. I see no problem with this.

> "It is useful against Malkavians, so who cares whether it is "needed"."

> So are many other non specific strategies that do not rely on either
> luckily being next to a Malkavian or knowning before you play that you
> will.

As I have said, I have never played hosers out of prior knowledgee. I
have played them for fun, knowing I might have to discard them. I have
never set out to hose a specific Malkavian player (and if I did, it would
be his fault for letting me know what he was playing).

I love to play Nossies, and, when I finally get my hands on a "Nosferatu
Performance Art" I will certainly include one in my next Nossie
deck...just because we Nossies hate the Toreador (who like to intercept us
and disrupt our strategy). I shall probably have to discard the card, of
course, but I'd like to see the look on my opponent's face when I *do* use
it.

Just for fun, I think I would like to construct a Nosferatu "Toreador
Hoser" Deck, complete with lots of Tragic Love Affairs and Nosferatu
Performance Arts. Then I will wait for a good opportunity to use it. If
my opponent complains that it is "lame" or "unfair" then he just has no
sense of humor, now does he?

> "I can remember a time when posters on this ng were lamenting the power
> of Malkavians, and saying "Thank God for Malkavian Dementia""

> Yes. Because they didn't really understand the game (myself included).

That's an odd statement. I would still use the card if there were not so
many clans in the game, or if it also effected Malk Antitribu. Is this
because I don't understand the game? Or is it perhaps because my play
style, and my game environment, have been somewhat different from yours?

> "I don't think you get this card at all. It can be quite useful, and also fun,
> even if you are not trying to "hose" the Malkavian player."

> No, I understand the card perfectly. I play it on your untapped Malkavian, use
> him to diablerize your other torporized Malkavian, and call a blood hunt on the
> first Malkavian. You now have had 2 vampires burned with very little
> effort/cost on my part. This is pretty much what has happened every single
> time I have played Malkavian Dementia.

Good for you. I personally would play the card in multiplayer games to
get free actions for myself. I would not necessarily be using it to
severely damage an opponent because I would be unlikely that the Malkavian
opponent was my prey.

> ""Seeds of Corruption" comes to mind, as, while it is particularly
> useful against Settites, it is still useful even if none are on the table."

> Exactly. Seeds of Corruption is a perfectly acceptable card, as it is not
> highly situational. The Clan Hosers as a whole are incedibly sketchy, as
> again, they are not worth including in your deck unless you know you will be
> playing against a certain clan, and if you put them in your deck because you
> know you are going to be playing against said clan, you are gaining an unfair
> advantage.

Well, I agree that any new "hosers" that are designed should be made less
situational. I already see some attempt to do this. For istance "Jackal"
can be used against two clans, not one. It is still probably too
situational, but the idea is a step in the right direction. "Anti-Sect"
cards are another step in this direction--less situational (as there are
only 3 sects), but the same concept nonetheless.

No no, he's not saying that clan hosers are 'bad' or 'poorly compatible
with the game design' because they're wallpaper. He's saying that they
don't seem to fit into the game design philosophy that applied to the
rest of the cardset. The basic design principle of Jyhad (at least back
in the day) seemed to be 'appropriate cost for effect' and 'every card
should be fairly useful'. There really isn't much wallpaper in the
original set, and most of the cards are pretty fair in terms of not
being blatantly overpowered.

The problem Peter (and I, I guess) has with clan hosers is that they
punish your opponent for showing up with a vampire belonging to a
particular clan. In a world where no clan is inherently better than
the others, this seems to be somewhat 'unfair' or at least not very
nice. Basically, the idea here is that 'color screw' cards are not
an appropriate solution for anything. Once everyone sits down with
their decks, they have no control over what clans of vampires they
can bring out; it seems wrong to punish them for having selected a
clan for which you happen to be packing the hoser.

most powerful clan in the base set. At least in no limits games,
Ventrue Vote and Rush Combat decks have appeared at least as effective
in my experience.)

: environment when he designes his deck. If one's opponents have lots of

I really don't want to have to quote everything said about Clan Hosers, but I
will add my own arguments. I feel that they are good for the game, and
perhaps even necessary, for the following reasons:

First off, flavour. In V:TM, each clan has a weakness. The Assamite
weakness is built into their vampires. The weaknesses of all other clans are
represented by their "Hoser" card. Malkavians are random and quick to change
their minds. The fact that they are the strongest clan (and I purposefully
do not qualify that with "under 4 CL" or "in the original set") is certainly
at odds with their personalities. In V:TM, a Malk can be powerful and scary,
but their Derangements ultimately keep them from being as devastating as
their discipline set could make them. Thus, we have Malk Dementia. And, at
least in my playgroup, when Malk decks were in vogue, Dementia's appeared to
counteract them. Similarly, when Gangrel Freaky-bleed decks were in style
(before NRA), Gangrel De-evolution checked it. In fact, Gangrel De-ev was
very popular for a while, since most of the Gangrel decks around here liked
bruise and bleed, leaving Bum's Rush and Haven Uncovered for the Brujah and
Caitiff.

So, actually, this is part of my second point, balance. I, for one, do not
believe that all the clans are balanced. It's my strong opinion that
Malkavians, Gangrel, and Ventrue have advantages over other clans. In 4CL,
Malks rule easily. In NL, they're not as bad, but I still consider them the
most powerful. And so, if there is a strong shift in the metagame, such that
people notice the superiority of the clans, and start using these clans more,
then the "Hosers" start popping up. And when a Ventrue deck is winning
constantly, you have some recourse. If this punishes anything, it punishes
uncreativity. If you use a deck with Giovanni, Nosferatu, and Tzimices,
you're unlikely to get any clan hosers hurting you. But if you play mono-
Ventrue *and* win all the time, you've got to expect Cultivated Blood
Shortage to pop up, or even Triole's Revenge, if you're really unlucky. If
there's one thing I hate, it's a one-clan deck. Sure, I've played them
before, and I'll play them again, but if clan hosers were stronger, I
wouldn't. Generally, my one-clan decks are Tremere Antitribu, and Infamous
Warlock is probably *the* worst clan hoser.

The third reason is this... say you've constructed a deck that is pretty
good, but it always gets beaten by a certain type of deck... Say you have a
Giovanni bruise-and-bleed with second round agg damage. Well, if your prey's
a Tremere, you're not gonna get very far. If you're lucky enough to make it
to the second round, you're just to going to get a Walk of Flame shoved in
your face. So, maybe you throw in a couple of Letters from Vienna, and hope
those nasty Tremere can't Wake. Or say you've got a slow-developing Brujah
stealth-bleed deck (I do...). If your predator's bleeding you with
Malkavians for 10 pool a turn, you need some protection. So you put in a
couple of Malk Dementia's and use the Malks to your advantage.

The best reason is the Lasombra. The Lasombra are just plain better than
everyone else (at least in their opinion), so if they can't make a deck full
of nothing but Clan Hosers, then I just don't want to play this game.
Couldn't you just see it... the only ones to stand a chance would be the
Tremere and Anti-Tremere. Well... and I suppose the Assamites and Ravnos,
since they don't really have a hoser card. 8)

Robert Goudie wrote:

"I'll have to disagree that they are contrary to the original design
paradigm. I do know where you are coming from though. I'd say the
master phase is the portion of the game that most resembles MtG. The Clan
hosers are the equivalent of the MtG "protection from color x" type cards.
Also, in the Master phase you see things like Sudden Reversal and now Direct
Intervention which have the most obvious relation to the "Counterspell" in MtG.
The minion cards have a completely different paradigm than the masters."

All in all, I suppose you are correct. I have, howver, always thought that
Color Hosers in Magic were particularly wack and that Sudden reversal was also
out of place in Jyhad :-)

"I don't believe clan hosers are bad in either case. The risk of putting in a
useless hoser is balanced with the benefit derived from such a card. From a
strategy standpoint, the proper place for Clan Hosers is again, the Meta Game.
If you can accurately predict what others will play, then it might be worth
adding the hoser. Also, I routinely add Malk Dementia when my library
selection would work well with a demented Malk."

My view of Clan Hosers is that they give a huge advantage for having non game
specific knowledge--i.e. if I know that you like to play Malkavians, and I show
up playing with 6 Malk Dementias, I am gaining a pretty substantial advantage
that far outweighs the cost of 6 card slots in my deck. Clan hosers are
balanced out by their incredibly specific use. If that cost is nullified
(because you know your opponents are playing a certain clan beforehand), then
the cards become far more powerful than they should be--their cost (that of
opportunity) is no longer sufficient for their power. In a situation where
there is no ability to know for sure that you will be facing a particular clan
(like in a tournament, for instance), the opportunity cost of these cards is
appropriate. Without the opportunity cost, Clan Hosers become (IMO) far more
powerful than their cost warrants.

I prefer the meta game swing to affect deck strategy, rather than which Hoser
Cards you cycle into your deck. If you can accurately predict what kinds of
decks your opponents will be playing, you can adjust your deck strategy to deal
with them.

All in all though, most of the Clan Hosers are pretty useless even if you know
that a particular clan will be at the table. Malkavian Dementia is an
exception, as it tends to make Malkavians dissapear, not just waste an action
or two (Out of Control is another noteable exception).

outweighed by their cost when said cost (of opportunity) is nullified by
outside of game knowledge, like Malkavian Dementia tends to be. An exception

News), which are generally considered too powerful in general.

clans in the game, or if it also effected Malk Antitribu. Is this because I

environment, have been somewhat different from yours?"

group, until everyone starts browbeating people out of playing them, or play
Malkavian Dementia enough to demoralize them. This is not because the
Malkavians are too powerful. It is because it is alot easier to understand how
to play them then it is how to deal with them. Once a good understanding of
Bum's Rush combat takes a hold in a play group, the Malkavians become
considerably less effective. When players build decks that can deal with
Malkavians (and still be perfectly viable regardless of whether or not
Malkavians are around), Malkavian Dementia tends to be over kill.

> pretentious."
>

> Umm, dude, settle down just a bit. If you cannot discuss silly card games
> without resorting insults, you had better re-examine your priorities a bit.

OK. You're right, and I appologize.

If I may restate somewhat, I do feel that your statements have lacked a
certain humility of perspective. You seem to assume that there is one
single game environment (or "metagame" as I have heard it called)--that of
the hypothetical "experienced gamer" (exemplified by you, I presume)--and
that cards which find little use in this environment are therefore
"incompatible with game design".

But there are many game environements, or "metagames", and it is hard to
totally predict which cards will or will not be worth putting in a deck.
It does seem a mite lacking in humility to imply, as you do, that if
someone puts clan hosers in a deck it is because he (or his companions) do
not know how to play.

But much of what you say is true. The clan hosers are in fact very
specific, or situational, and this is increasingly becoming a problem due
to the proliferation of clans. Thus it is less likely than for most cards
that you will find a game environment, or "metagame" where they are worth
putting in a deck. One poster just mentioned that Gangrel Atavism was
useful in an environment where Gangrel Freaky Bleed Decks are common.
This is certainly something I never thought of, and just goes to show that
one should be cautious when making absolutist statements that certain
cards are always a bad idea.

> It is hardly an inappropriate check on the most powerful clan in the original
> set, and certainly never stopped them from winning more than their fair share
> of games and tournaments."

> The Malkavians are no more powerful than any other of the basic set

> clans. Just sit a Malk S+B deck next to an effective Bum's Rush deck,
> and see who gets to be "Rock".

I have personally never played a Malkavian Stealth Bleed deck (except for
a poorly focussed one I constructed carelessly out of my pile of excess
cards--which worked suprisingly well.) I think I may try to create a
determinedly dangerous one for the next tournament, and see how it works.
(I normally play Nossies, and some very non-standard decks). It should
not be too hard to give the Malks some combat defence.

> Under 4CL, the Malkavians are very powerful, as they are completely

> unhindered by the card limit. Under NL (as the game was designed), the

> Malkavians are fairly easy to build effective decks out of, but they are

> in no way "the most powerful clan in the original set".

I don't approve of 4CL on the whole, but what you say about it does
illustrate the point that not all game environments are the same. In
fact, a 4CL-type game environment can be mimicked in situations where a
formal 4CL limit is not enforced, such as a situation where the players
have a limitted number of cards to choose from and don't happen to have a
dozen of each uncommon available to them. Some game groups might not have
that many cards apiece, and even experienced players might agree to play
decks constructed from a few sealed starter packs. In such a situation,
including Malk Dementia is your deck is hardly a bad idea, even if you are
an experienced player.

> Malkavian Dementia is too powerful in a situation where the cost (the large
> possibility that it will be useless due to no Malkavians) is nullified (you
> know your opponent will be using the Malkavian). In this situation, the cost
> no longer justifies the ability of the card.

The setup of the game is that you are not supposed to know what one's
opponent is playing until well after each of you has chosen their decks.
Thus, in theory, there should never be a situation where you *know* your
opponent is playing Malkavian. If you can guess this, that is your
opponents fault for being too predictable. Players are always trying to
outguess eachother. It is part of the game.

The power of Malkavian Dementia is offset by the likelyhood that it will
be useless and jam your hand, and this is becoming increasingly true
with proliferation of the number of clans.

> A large portion of the above cards are mostly useless, due to their
> incredibly specific nature. However, the abilities of these cards
> generally are not outweighed by their cost when said cost (of
> opportunity) is nullified by outside of game knowledge, like Malkavian
> Dementia tends to be. An exception to this are the cards that outright
> destroy vampires (like Malkavian Dementia tends to do), such as Archon
> Investigation (for which there are veritable volumes of posts debating
> the appropriateness of this card. Check out Deja News), which are
> generally considered too powerful in general.

What sort of "outside of game" knowledge are you talking about. I always
thought it was an accepted aspect of the game that it is dangerous to let
your opponent know what deck you are playing.

> "Then I will wait for a good opportunity to use it. If my opponent
> complains that it is "lame" or "unfair" then he just has no sense of
> humor, now does he?"

> That is certainly an matter of opinion. I suspect that your opponent

> will think he has a fine sense of humor, but will still be miffed that
> you sat down at a table and took out a deck designed specifically to
> kill him.

What else is my deck supposed to be designed for? What's he going to say:
"Damn it, I trusted you, and told you what clan I was playing, but you
tricked me and hosed me you no good filthy undead bloodsucking vampire!"

When I sit down with a friend for a one-to-one game, we hose eachother's
decks all the time. "Hey, do you still have that Nossie Weenie Wall deck
you played last week? I've come up with a deck that can hose it." "OK,
lets see what you can do." In such one-on-one play, the "metagame"
becomes extremely specific, since it is not tempered by an average of a
large number of decks. I hope you will not now instruct me that Jyhad was
not designed for this type of play, and that this sort of fun is somehow
illigitimate.

Seriously, I play Nossies with distressing regularity (at least half the
time). If my opponents wise up and put Whispers of the Niktuku in their
decks, whose fault is it but mine? So far, no one has come after me that
way, but if I were to win often enough with Nossies, and others began
following my example, I am sure they would. Oh well. Guess I'd have to
try another clan.

> "That's an odd statement. I would still use the card if there were not
> so many clans in the game, or if it also effected Malk Antitribu. Is
> this because I don't understand the game? Or is it perhaps because my
> play style, and my game environment, have been somewhat different from
> yours?"

> Most beginning players of Jyhad quickly discover that the Malkavians are

> pretty easy to make effective decks out of. The Malkavians then
> dominate the play group, until everyone starts browbeating people out of
> playing them, or play Malkavian Dementia enough to demoralize them.
> This is not because the Malkavians are too powerful. It is because it
> is alot easier to understand how to play them then it is how to deal
> with them. Once a good understanding of Bum's Rush combat takes a hold
> in a play group, the Malkavians become considerably less effective.

I'm sure there is much truth to this analysis, as long as one realizes it
is merely a generalization of the incredible complexity of "metagame"
flux. None of it applies in any absolute sense.

The above apparently concedes that there *are* certain metagames
(specifically, some "beginning player" metagames) in which Malkavian
Dementia is a useful card. You are apparently conceding, that, in such
game environments, Malkavians *are* too powerful and predominant, and that
Malkavian Dementia can be an appropriate counter for those who don't have
8 in every card.

I think you should also concede that Jyhad consists of innumerable
metagames, and that certain hoser cards could in fact be useful in certain
game environments, even for experienced players. You cannot anticipate
all possible game environments.

The clan hosers may have failed to contribute to the game to the extent
that they should, but I feel they hardly distract from it.

Suppose I were to construct a Settite Temptation deck. I would probably
include at leat one Malkavian Dementia, since that fits perfectly will
with this theme. If no-one played Malkavians, I would simply discard it.

> When players build decks that can deal with Malkavians (and still be
> perfectly viable regardless of whether or not Malkavians are around),
> Malkavian Dementia tends to be over kill.

Actually, when players build decks that can deal with Malkavians (and
still be perfectly viable regardless of whether Malkavians are around),
then people will tend to avoid Malkavians, and Malkavian Dementia will
become useless. The "metagame" is constantly shifting.

Now, on the the game!

This was never my point, and if it came across as such, I apologize. My
statements about Malkavian Dementia being viewed as an attempt to balance out
the Malkavians was based on the fairly common belief by newer players that the
Malkavians are too powerful. When I started playing Jyhad, our play group felt
the exact same way, and put 4 MD in every deck we made, and still kept getting

what we were doing wrong, and now our play group looks at the Malkavians like
most other effective clans--useful, but not overpowered.

"It should not be too hard to give the Malks some combat defence."

Against determined combat decks, it is pretty difficult(By determined, I mean
pure Rush combat that is prepared to deal with S:CE and Dodges, and designed to
put an opponent into torpor with every attack). All the Malks have (in clan
disciplines) are Thoughts Betrayed and Obedience. For TB, you need superior
DOM and 2 blood, and enough of them to be constantly available. With
Obediance, you need to be older then the attacking vampire and untapped/packing
Wakes. It isn't impossible to use them, but if you load your deck with
Obediance, TB, and Wakes, and then you end up next to a non combat deck, you
will be incredibly hand jammed, as is always a risk.

"What sort of "outside of game" knowledge are you talking about. I always
thought it was an accepted aspect of the game that it is dangerous to let your
opponent know what deck you are playing."

I'm ususally talking about your general play group. In my standard play group,
It is fairly likely that I will be playing the Nosferatu (I always play the
Nosferatu...), fairly likely that Josh will be playing the Brujah, and fairly
likely that Dave will be playing the Ventrue. As a result, if I put Ventrue
hosers and Brujah hosers in my deck when I go to play with Josh and Dave, it is
highly likely that they will be useful (much like Nosferatu hosers are highly
likely to be useful against me...). Thus, the cost of the hoser cards
(opportunity cost) is nullified by the fact that I know I'll be playing with
Josh and Dave, who like to use particular clans. In a tournament situation
(where you are playing blind) I'm all for clan hosers, as they have a cost. In
freindly play with your standard Jyhad pals, they generally no longer have a
cost.

"I hope you will not now instruct me that Jyhad was not designed for this type
of play, and that this sort of fun is somehow illigitimate."

I claim no such thing. If you guys enjoy yourselves, by all means, go to town.
All along, I have been stating my opinion, which is that clan hosers are
unaccpetable in non blind play, due to their lack of appropriate cost, and as a
result, they were a poor addition to the game. It is simply my opinion.

"None of it applies in any absolute sense."

Again, I never claimed that any of my opinions were in any way absolute, simply
my opinions.

I have lurked on this discussion a long time (it is a long thread) and I
think that this is the main point. Picture your local playgroup. One
person *always* plays the same clan. You are sick of it, as they never
change their deck, and to an experienced player, the true joy of Jyhad
is to see exactly how bizarre a deck can be that still (partially)
works.

To "encourage" the player to understand the true joy of variety, include
the clan hosers. They will swiftly become annoyed with you, but in the
long term, they will thank you, for moving them away from the path of
true boredom onto the path of enlightenment.

In short, clan hosers encourage variety in play for a local group. To
"encourage" someone to try a new deck, you can either build a deck
specifically to kill that annoying little deck, or (much more simply)
just include a few hosers in the deck you are about to build.

HOSERS = VARIETY = LONGEVITY

Praise to the hosers.

David Naseby

On 18 Feb 1998, Joshua Duffin wrote:

> No no, he's not saying that clan hosers are 'bad' or 'poorly compatible
> with the game design' because they're wallpaper.

To my mind, this is the only way they *are* 'bad' or 'poorly compatible'.
to the extent that anyone can figure a way to make use of them, I think
they are fine.

> He's saying that they
> don't seem to fit into the game design philosophy that applied to the
> rest of the cardset. The basic design principle of Jyhad (at least back
> in the day) seemed to be 'appropriate cost for effect' and 'every card
> should be fairly useful'. There really isn't much wallpaper in the
> original set, and most of the cards are pretty fair in terms of not
> being blatantly overpowered.
>
> The problem Peter (and I, I guess) has with clan hosers is that they
> punish your opponent for showing up with a vampire belonging to a
> particular clan. In a world where no clan is inherently better than
> the others, this seems to be somewhat 'unfair' or at least not very
> nice.

I still don't get you. How is this any different from putting a dog pack
in my gangrel deck to "punish" a player who uses S:CE instead of dodges?
How is it different from putting a Far Mastery in ones deck to "punish"
the player who brings out Renegade Garous and then equips them with Flak
Jackets and Bastard Swords. How is it different from using Ancilla
Empowerment, Ebenezer Rousch, and Muddled Vampire Hunter to hose them
weenie decks? And since when are Methuselah's supposed to be "nice" to
each other?

> Basically, the idea here is that 'color screw' cards are not
> an appropriate solution for anything. Once everyone sits down with
> their decks, they have no control over what clans of vampires they
> can bring out; it seems wrong to punish them for having selected a
> clan for which you happen to be packing the hoser.

Does it also seem wrong to punish them for putting cards in their library
that don't happen to work against yours? Besides, it is perfectly
acceptable to have more than one clan in your crypt, and you *do* have
some control over which vampires you choose to bring out.

Sometimes I get upset when I play my "Wynn" deck or my "Lucretia" deck or
my "Democritus" deck, and find that the vampire I built my deck around
becomes contested. How is this any different?

An enormous part of the game will always be deck design. Skill of play
will count for alot, but some decks just don't work right against others
or in a certain play environment. A deck that may be well designed for
one "metagame" may be poorly designed for another. If you don't think
this is as it should be, you would have to fix alot more than the clan
hosers. You'd have to design a totally different game.

> (regarding Malk Dementia - I would disagree that the Malks were the
> most powerful clan in the base set. At least in no limits games,
> Ventrue Vote and Rush Combat decks have appeared at least as effective
> in my experience.)

The Malks *were* the most powerful clan in the basic set. There is no
such thing as a "no limit" play environment, as no players I have an
unlimited number of cards. The cards that make Malks powerful are common,
numerous and readily available. This is a real and ongoing advantage,
which one cannot completely ignore by wishfully imagining that we all,
(and especially any newer players) have an unlimited number of all
uncommons and rares.

I think many are also forgetting the enormous extent that combat decks
were enhanced by the change in Aggravated Damage rules. (BTW, while I
like the fact that combat has been enhanced, I do not like the effect of
the new rules on the game atmosphere. In the old game, there was a real
sense that vampires were immortal, and near impossible to kill, and that
the best one could normally do was put them out of action for a while. You
could kill them, by committing diablerie, but it was a serious and
dangerous crime. In the new game they are constantly being burned with
impunity. Diablerie and the bloodhunt vote have fallen by the wayside as
significant elements of the game).

> : Lets not leave out variety, originality, unpredictability, atmosphere, and
> : fun.
>
> All of these things are great, but in terms of game mechanics, I don't
> think they're really the goal. Balance and playability are (should be)
> the goals.

Well, yes, I admit that many of the clan hosers have turned out to have
minimum playability (too specific, as Peter said), but they have not
adversely affected balance. To the extent that they have turned out to be
playable, I cannot see your objections to them.

> I snipped out everything not from the original set (Jyhad); there are
> twelve cards you list here that I agree are basically wallpapery due
> to depending so much on what your opponents are playing. That's out
> of at least three hundred cards, I believe.

From the Jyhad set:
1. Betrayer
2. Brujah Frenzy
3. Cultivated Blood Shortage
4. Gangrel De-evolution
5. Illegal Search and Siezure
6. Letter from Vienna
7. Police Department
8. Rotschreck
9. Storm Sewers
10. Tragic Love Affair
11. Unnatural Disaster
12. Arson
13. Delaying Tactics
14. Dread Gaze
15. Elder Kindred Network
16. Far Mastery
17. Fast Hands
18. Flesh of Marble
19. Nosferatu Putrescence
20. Open Grate
21. Political Backlash
22. Pulling Strings
23. Rampage
24. Shattering Blow
25. Surprise Influence
26. Disputed Territory
27. Kindred Segregation
28. Praxis: Solomon

I think that makes about 9% of the minion card set. I concede that many
of them are minimally useful, some more than others, depending on the
extent that what they are designed to hose have become a significant part
of the game. Anti-location cards are less "wallpaperish" than anti-weapon
cards, because locations have become more a part of the game than weapons.
Anti-press cards are, as you point out, total wallpaper, because presses
have almost completely fallen by the wayside because of the excessive
power of S:CE. Cards that hose S:CE, however, are extremely valued, and
when Dog Pack came out in the Sabbat set, I don't remember anyone
complaining about the inappropriateness of its specificity. It is
possible that future cards in future sets ( :( ) will further reduce the
power of S:CE, and increase the value of press and anti-press, and Open
Grate will no longer be wallpaper.

Honorable mention to
29. Immortal Grapple: Only useful if opponent plays strike cards
or weapons. The press it grants at superior is the only thing that saves
it from being on the above list (and it's not like anyone plays this for
the press at superior).
30. Night Moves: It is not, as you pointed out, unusable, but
why put it in a deck when you can play a host of +1 stealth cards that
would not reduce your bleed... unless you suspect your opponents have
serious intercept?
31. Canine Horde: Yes, it can be used for 1R damage, but one
would never pick it over Aid from Bats unless you believe your opponent
has equipment.
32. Skin of Night: The superior version can be used for damage
prevention, but is inferior to numerous other fortitude damage prevention
cards. The card's usefulness depends almost entirely on one's opponent
playing aggravated damage.
33. Skin of Steel: The Skin of Steel/Pulled Fangs combo is the
only thing (in the original set) that prevents this card's usefulness from
being entirely dependent on what one's opponent plays. Otherwise, it is
an expensive and pointless way to prevent normal cardless hand slaps
(since you lose a blood anyway, and can't play it if you don't have a
blood).
34. Blood Rage: I guess the superior version is approximately
equivalent to a Lucky Blow, except that it cannot be combined with other
bonuses. The inferior version is completely pointless unless your
opponent plays weapons or fortitude damage prevention.

> : The clan hosers listed above are in no way out of spirit with the game,
> : and are no different in spirit than many of the cards listed above. I

Yes. It's also real obnoxious the way those Gangrel keep trying to
convince me to add combat defence by torporizing my vamps, or those
Ventrue encourage me to have intercept by voting me to death, or those
Malks encourage me to have bleed defence by bleeding me dry. It's also
rude the way those presence-misdirection decks try to convince me to put
WWEF in my deck. If they were to kindly explain to me on the error of my
ways, I think it would be alot more appropriate. :)

> : specifically to kill that annoying little deck, or (much more simply)
> : just include a few hosers in the deck you are about to build.
>
> Well, if you don't like the person very much, sure... ;-)

Most of us who play Jyhad are adults. We expect our opponents to try to
win by any means possible, and it is perfectly acceptable to make an
educated guess about what they expect you to have in your hand or crypt.

Personally, I am flattered when the table gangs up on my (especially when
they all come after me in a tournament's final round), as it means they
regard me as a threat. If someone in my playgroup were to add Nossie
hosers, I would take that as a complement--it would mean I had actually
managed to turn the underpowered Nossies into a threat. If people were to
begin playing Nossie clan hosers consistently, I would be filled with
pride beyond belief.

> Maybe I'm just naive, but it seems to me that most people would
> wind up happier and more encouraged if you tried explaining to them
> verbally what's boring about what they're doing, and why they should
> try doing something else for the sake of variety.

I'm sorry, but that does sound naive. I fully expect my fellow
methuselahs to screw me any way they can (and that includes punishing me
for predictability). However, if they started giving me condescending
lectures about how boring they think I am, I might be kinda miffed.

I have no patience for the use of moral suasion to shame others out of
playing "cheesy decks" like Malkavian S&B, especially since this is one of
the few decks that Newbie players can be competitive with. If your newbie
player starts winning consistently with Malkavians, then the appropriate
and respectable way to show him the error of his ways is to tear off the
kid gloves and start hosing him (using clan hosers or any other technique
designed specifically to deal with him). He may be forced to design a new
deck, but at least he has the satisfaction of knowing that he has been
treated as a threat and has had an effect on the play environment.

If this newbie were, on the other hand, to recieve condescending lectures
on creativity from players with alot more cards than he, he might very
well go away and never return.

> Also, I'm not sure that it's really anyone else's responsibility to
> make sure that I'm excited during a game of Jyhad.

I agree to an extent (and I think David was being a little facetious about
that part). I think the point is that Clan Hosers do tend to promote
creativity and variety. This is true even if you just play them to win,
in an effort to use your opponents predicability to your own advantage.

> If I find someone's
> deck boring, I can certainly tell them so and whine about it if I
> want, but it seems to me that it's pretty much their right to play
> any deck that makes them happy. Even if I think it's uncreative and
> stupid. If I'm concerned about variety and wacky ideas, I can always
> try them out myself.

Yes, but you also have a right to use your opponent's predictability
against him.

> Of course, it's nice if you can get your playgroup to think the same
> way you do in terms of variety and what is the appropriate level of
> 'playing to win' type behavior.

I don't think there is an enormous dichotomy between "playing to win" and
playing for fun and variety. The creative player may occasionally play
wacky decks that he does not expect to win, but in the long run he learns
more about the game and wins more often. He also makes it harder for his
opponents to predict his hand.

> But clan hosers, if you ask me, look
> like a very blunt instrument for behavior modification. Kinda like
> opening doors with a sledgehammer or something.

They are just an instrument by which a player may be punished for being
too consistent, especially if he is consistently winning. They are just
one (small) part of how the basic game design encourages creativity and
variety.

in terms of cost versus effect. The ones on the higher end of the
power curve (e.g. Malkavian Dementia, Out of Control (a burn-an-Anti-
Brujah of some maximal size master) don't cost enough (a card and a
master card action, usually) for what they do.

It's true that they only work if someone has a vampire of the
appropriate clan. But I don't think that's enough of a restriction
to justify the cost reduction these cards seem to enjoy (Letter from
Vienna - like a Misdirection that costs 0 instead of X; the Malkavian

card.

I guess, as in the one where the Malks became too powerful and popular
due to a limited card pool - but even in a situation like that, it

"29. Immortal Grapple: Only useful if opponent plays strike cards or weapons.
The press it grants at superior is the only thing that saves it from being on
the above list (and it's not like anyone plays this for the press at

I can only assume that your particular playgroup does not have a heavy combat
environment, leading to your particular view on many of these cards. This is
not a judgement (nor am I attempting to imply that I am in any way more
advanced a player as a result of this statement), but many of the cards you
mentioned in the above list were incredibly important cards in a high/efficient
combat environment. Immortal Grapple, in particular, is a key card in any
Potence combat deck, as it prevents the use of: S:CE, Dodge, Guns, Weapons,
Thaumaturgy strikes, Viscicitude strikes, and basically anything that isn't a
hand strike. Without Immortal Grapple, Potence combat simply is not a viably
concept.

"Focus on superior Obfuscate rather than superior Dominate. They have
Swallowed by the Night, a stealth card that can also be used to maneuver to
long range. Behind You is under-rated. "

It just won't work out that well. Again, a good combat deck is a deck that is
designed to successfully put its opponent into torpor with every attack, and if
it cannot deal with some manuvers and dodges, it simply is not worth playing.
An effective combat deck will either have plenty of manuvers (the Brujah with
Flash), plenty of presses (the Gangrel with Trap), or some schtick like Drawing
out the Beast, otherwise, the deck will just not be effective. In actual
practice, any combat deck that does not rely heavily upon either Immortal
Grapple or Psyche! will simply not work all that well (Decks that use Hidden
Lurker, Fast Reaction, or Thoughts Betrayed can be effective as well, but tend
to be a bit trickier) Loading a Malkavian deck with Manuvers (I always liked
Behind You, myself, but for Nosferatu manuvers, so I could Immortally Grapple
my opponents...) makes them work a bit harder, but it just won't work against a
good rush deck.

The Elisium and Mariel are very important to a Malk deck, but the Elisium is
pretty fragile, and Mariel tends to die very quickly.

"What I still don't understand is, if this is in the situation, why do you not
use clan hosers? If you were to do so, why would it be unfair?"

The situation is this: Our playgroup is a bunch of over analytical game
critics who have been playing Jyhad since it was invented. In our overly
thought out view of the game, in a situation where you are likely to know what
clan your opponents will be playing, clan hosers tend to be too effective for
their cost, as their inherrent cost is nullified. In reality, only a few of
the clan hosers really suffer from this (Malk Dementia, Out of Control and a
few others), but as a result of these few, we just don't use clan hosers. The
end issue is cost vs. effectiveness. Malk Dementia (and Out of Control) is
just too effective for its completely negligible cost.

"It seems to me that your playgroup has an unspoken agreement that no-one will
do anything to interfere with eachother's regularly playing their favorite
clan."

No, we have a spoken agreement to not use Clan Hosers for the above reasons.
The lack of clan hosers in no way impedes our deck construction, and in no way
impedes our strategy decisions, as clan hosers are just too random to have an
effect of design considerations.

"If you know something about the play style of the participants, you are
certainly entitled to use this to your advantage, and this applies to alot of
things besides clan hosers."

Yes, but clan hosers are, again, far too effective for their incredibly limited
cost, where most other situational cards just are not. Again, it is mostly
Malk Dementia (as for one master phase and one card, you generally manage to
destroy a vampire or two), but you can't curse one clan hoser and not curse
tham all.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Lupus Australius wrote:

(in response to the Immortal Grapple/other situational non-clan hoser cards)

"I don't think you're getting me. I never expressed an opinion of this card at
all. Obviously I agree that it is a very useful and effective card. The
reason it is (almost) on the list is because the list is of cards whose
usefulness depends on what cards one's opponent is playing."

I got that part, but as opposed to Clan hosers, Immortal Grapple is always
useful. There is no situation where it cannot be played (barring an inabbility
to get into a fight, but then you are just screwed...) and will not help in
some way if you are playing a Potence combat deck. If your predator or prey
(or grand predator or grand prey) have zero combat cards in their deck, you can
still use them just to cycle your hand, as well as using it for the press (I
use the Press at superior all the time). For instance, I play a Nosferatu
combat deck that relies very heavily on its 9 Immortal Grapples. Without them,
the deck would be completely non-viable, as the it would be shut down by S:CE
and Dodge. If my opponents are playing zero combat cards, then I can play the
IG (multiple times in a single combat if need be) to gain presses and just to
cycle my hand. Immortal Grapple is the very basis of the entire deck, and
without it, the deck would just not work on a grand scale. Sure, occasionally
it would kill stuff without the Immortal Grapples, but more often than not, my
opponents would play the incredibly common S:CE or just dodge, and I would just
sit around and do nothing.

That is the difference between cards like Immortal Grapple and clan hosers.
You cannot build an effective deck strategy around clan hosers. They are too
random and situational to rely on (and they clog your hand when you can't use
them). Occasionally, if they are in your deck, you will gain an advantage from
them, but you simply cannot build a deck and say, "Oh, this deck here would not
work without its Letter From Viennas." Immortal Grapple and Skin of Steel are
often the very basis of deck strategy.

"It is less specific than other cards, but it's usefulness is still dependent
on what one's opponent has in their deck. Thus, in principle, it is no
different from other "hoser" type cards."

The principal, again, is fundamentally different. Immortal Grapple makes
certain deck strategies viably compettetive. Clan hosers simply do not have
the ability to do this. They are random bonuses, not design backbones.

(about Clan hosers and stuff)

"Perhaps not, but I intend to try it. You're making me want to defend the
honor of the much abused Malkavians, whom I have no experience playing."

It's worth trying, but unless someone has a good Rush deck, it won't really
matter.

minions employ Ghoul Retainers. When I am attacked, I whip out a Combat

No. I thought I made that pretty clear. In tournaments (when you don't know
who all your opponents are), clan hosers have a pretty severe cost--opportunity
and deck space. For instance, my Nosferatu combat deck only has 12 master
cards in it, and they are all pretty important. I can't really use any more
masters, as then they tend to jam my hand, so I 'd have to swap out some
important masters to put in clan hosers which may or may not be useful.

In my normal play group, however, if I am going to be playing with Howard, I
know my Malkavian Dementia will be useful, cause he only owns one deck.

"Out of Control doesn't seem so bad to me. It can only be used once in a game.
One can defend against it too."

I pay 2 pool and a master card. You lose a vampire. That is wrong.

"Nosferatu Performance Art: Now that seems dangerous. But again, the
opportunity cost is high."

Not if you know it is likely your opponents will be playing Toreador.

"Besides, all those Sabbat diabolists are scum anyway. I say burn the lot of
them! It's not like they have any respect for unlife or anything."

Heh heh :-)

"Really? Then why is there an agreement not to use them? Couldn't you just
decide "Lets not trust each other like friends, and instead try to screw each
other like Methuselahs". The only result would be that you would have to be
unpredictable about the clans you play."

Because not everyone in my playgroup has the ability to be unpredictable. Josh
and I have infinite cards and can make any decks we could possibly imagine.
Wampler and Ian are highschool kids with only enough cards to make one good
deck. If I were to say "Hmm...Wampler is probably going to be playing that
Ravanos deck again. It's the only deck he owns. I'd better put in all of my
Ravanos Hosers!", that would not be particularly fair. Howard only owns one
deck, a Malkavian Pro/Obf/Dom S+B deck. He doesn't play Jyhad enough to have
alot of cards and the manical drive (like myself) to change his deck every time
we play. Thus, if I were to put in Malkavian Dementias every time I was going
to play with Howard, I would be gaing a huge advantage (and probably inspiring
Howard to not play anymore). There are other people in our play group, and
there is a pretty good deck selection, but still, why should I punnish my less
well card endowed pals for wanting to play Jyhad with over
powered/undercosted/highly situational clan hosers for which there is no
defense?

You can defend against normal strategy with common cards. If I am afraid of
S+B. I use Deflection or Rush combat or pool gain or intercept. If I am afraid
of combat, I use S:CE or Dodge. If I am afraid of Immortal Grapple, I use
Fortitude. If I am afraid of votes, I use Delaying Tactics or Intercept. If I
am afraid of S:CE, I use IG or Psyche or Hidden Lurker. If I am afraid of
manuvers, I use Flash or Drawing out the Beast. If I am afraid of Malkavian
Dementia or Out of Control, however, there is no defense except for Sudden
Reversal (which won't even help against Brujah Frenzy), and you can't build a
deck strategy out of Sudden Reversal.

"Depends. Have you ever played a deck based on a well-equiped Renegade Garou?"

No. They just keep dying around here. The 5 Pool for 3 life lasts about one
strike phase.

Lupus Australis (jbwh...@dorsai.org) wrote:

[snip]
[I wrote]
: > Maybe I'm just naive, but it seems to me that most people would

Well, I'm not really arguing for condescending lectures. But I do
think that resorting to, for example, the use of clan hosers to punish

otherwise they'll win too often - shows an embarrassing inability
to simply make decks that can deal with the winning deck on a level

: playing "cheesy decks" like Malkavian S&B, especially since this is one of
: the few decks that Newbie players can be competitive with. If your newbie
: player starts winning consistently with Malkavians, then the appropriate

: If this newbie were, on the other hand, to recieve condescending lectures

He might just as well go away and not come back if people start piling
Malk Dementias on his head, especially if he's one of those people

I completely agree that you shouldn't have to shame anyone out of
playing anything; I don't think there are any very feasibly cheesy
Jyhad decks. (Except maybe the ones built around the expansion
broken cards, like Return to Innocence and Tomb of Rameses III...)
Beating the new Malkavian kid on the block by taking him seriously

Heh. It's kinda funny for me to get the 'playing to win' lecture.
