Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Lupus Australis (jbwh...@dorsai.org) wrote:

: On 18 Feb 1998, Joshua Duffin wrote:

: > No no, he's not saying that clan hosers are 'bad' or 'poorly compatible
: > with the game design' because they're wallpaper.

: To my mind, this is the only way they *are* 'bad' or 'poorly compatible'.
: to the extent that anyone can figure a way to make use of them, I think
: they are fine.

Hmmmm. Do you mean that you only have problems with cards that are
underpowered, not ones that are overpowered (for their costs etc)?
Or just that you don't think any clan hosers could fall into the
overpowered category?

: I still don't get you. How is this any different from putting a dog pack

: in my gangrel deck to "punish" a player who uses S:CE instead of dodges?
: How is it different from putting a Far Mastery in ones deck to "punish"
: the player who brings out Renegade Garous and then equips them with Flak
: Jackets and Bastard Swords. How is it different from using Ancilla
: Empowerment, Ebenezer Rousch, and Muddled Vampire Hunter to hose them
: weenie decks? And since when are Methuselah's supposed to be "nice" to
: each other?

Well, the way it's different is that the other ideas you mention
essentially punish the player for using a particular strategy, by
using cards that counter or work against that strategy. A clan hoser
doesn't do anything directly toward stopping someone from accomplishing
the goals of their deck or toward defending you from their attacks; it
just messes with their vampires.

I don't know if I can really explain the mindset I'm coming from here,
but I'll try anyway.

Being 'nice' isn't exactly the issue. But trying to specifically screw
someone over by using cards that only work against that person seems
somehow unfriendly (ie not in keeping with the concept of a 'friendly
game').

: An enormous part of the game will always be deck design. Skill of play

: will count for alot, but some decks just don't work right against others
: or in a certain play environment. A deck that may be well designed for
: one "metagame" may be poorly designed for another. If you don't think
: this is as it should be, you would have to fix alot more than the clan
: hosers. You'd have to design a totally different game.

This is true to some extent. But I think that Jyhad/VTES at least tries
to escape this difficulty. I don't know if you have any familiarity with
the Star Wars ccg, but in my experience, it is very possible to have the
Dark Side and Light Side players focus on sufficiently different parts
of the game that the cards they deploy will never directly interact with
each other. (For example, the Empire might be playing a deep-space
deck while the Rebels are playing a Tattooine planet-based deck.)

In Jyhad, every deck has some basic compatibility with every other deck.
If you guess poorly about what kinds of strategies the other players
will be using, you can end up with a lot of useless cards in your
library. But you always have at least the basic structure of the game
(cardless actions, vampires which are the most basic tool of gameplay,
etc) to go on, and you should certainly have some cards that will be
useful in any situation.

My point is that cards with very specific applicability do carry some
higher risk of being useless with them. But that doesn't mean that
it's appropriate to entirely recost them, as in the case of clan hosers
which seem to get greatly reduced costs for their effects.

: > (regarding Malk Dementia - I would disagree that the Malks were the

: > most powerful clan in the base set. At least in no limits games,
: > Ventrue Vote and Rush Combat decks have appeared at least as effective
: > in my experience.)

: The Malks *were* the most powerful clan in the basic set. There is no
: such thing as a "no limit" play environment, as no players I have an
: unlimited number of cards. The cards that make Malks powerful are common,
: numerous and readily available. This is a real and ongoing advantage,
: which one cannot completely ignore by wishfully imagining that we all,
: (and especially any newer players) have an unlimited number of all
: uncommons and rares.

The cards that beat Malks up are also common, numerous, and readily
available. Deflection. Bum's Rush. Fast Reaction. Hidden Lurker.
(Psyche and Immortal Grapple are much better but are rarer. I do, by
the way, think that a card as important as IG to the effectiveness of
combat decks should not have been a rare.) And Jyhad cards are so cheap
that it's not that pricey to get a lot of everything useful - as much as
you could reasonably want. Sure, you don't have an actually unlimited
number of cards, but I would never want to put more than a dozen of
most cards into a deck anyway.

: I think many are also forgetting the enormous extent that combat decks

: were enhanced by the change in Aggravated Damage rules. (BTW, while I
: like the fact that combat has been enhanced, I do not like the effect of
: the new rules on the game atmosphere. In the old game, there was a real
: sense that vampires were immortal, and near impossible to kill, and that
: the best one could normally do was put them out of action for a while. You
: could kill them, by committing diablerie, but it was a serious and
: dangerous crime. In the new game they are constantly being burned with
: impunity. Diablerie and the bloodhunt vote have fallen by the wayside as
: significant elements of the game).

While the agg-damage change did make it much easier to burn vampires,
that really doesn't help all combat decks. Potence strikes are usually
not agg. Pulled Fangs is now able to burn vamps, which it really
shouldn't be (I think), and that's significant. But combat didn't
become all *that* much more effective overall due to the agg-damage
change. (I do agree though that the old way was better, with vamps
being harder to simply burn via agg, making diablerie more widely
necessary.)

: Well, yes, I admit that many of the clan hosers have turned out to have

: minimum playability (too specific, as Peter said), but they have not
: adversely affected balance. To the extent that they have turned out to be
: playable, I cannot see your objections to them.

Well, I think some of them are overpowered, basically.

Also, personally I don't think they're 'fun' or 'creative' cards.

: > I snipped out everything not from the original set (Jyhad); there are

: > twelve cards you list here that I agree are basically wallpapery due
: > to depending so much on what your opponents are playing. That's out
: > of at least three hundred cards, I believe.

: From the Jyhad set:
: 9. Storm Sewers
: 13. Delaying Tactics

These two in particular I disagree about being wallpaper. I guess
maybe I should explain what I mean by wallpaper first. Obviously
every card is situationally dependent to some extent. Given that
bleed, vote, and combat are the three major strategies of Jyhad, I
think it's reasonably to expect these aspects of the game to show up
on a regular basis.

Given that, Storm Sewers has shown up in a Nosferatu combat deck fairly
often around here, as it guarantees close range if blocked, which
is handy for the Nosfers who are otherwise somewhat lacking in
maneuvers (and who, when playing Immortal Grapple potence combat, want
very much to be at close range).

Delaying Tactics is the best vote defense I know of which is neither
outvoting the voter (ie having too many votes of your own on the table
to be a viable target for being harmed by voting) or intercepting the
votes.

: I think that makes about 9% of the minion card set. I concede that many

: of them are minimally useful, some more than others, depending on the
: extent that what they are designed to hose have become a significant part
: of the game. Anti-location cards are less "wallpaperish" than anti-weapon
: cards, because locations have become more a part of the game than weapons.
: Anti-press cards are, as you point out, total wallpaper, because presses
: have almost completely fallen by the wayside because of the excessive
: power of S:CE. Cards that hose S:CE, however, are extremely valued, and
: when Dog Pack came out in the Sabbat set, I don't remember anyone
: complaining about the inappropriateness of its specificity. It is
: possible that future cards in future sets ( :( ) will further reduce the
: power of S:CE, and increase the value of press and anti-press, and Open
: Grate will no longer be wallpaper.

Actually, Dog Pack (Ancient Hearts if I remember right - the Gangrel
retainer that prevents the opposing minion from playing S:CE etc) suffers
not only from being ultra hard to come by (as it was a rare) but also
from being very specific in its application. In other words, it can
be hard to justify paying two pool and taking an action to be able
to avoid S:CE in future combats, even when you're the Gangrel, who
have no other good in-clan way of dealing with S:CE.

: Honorable mention to

: 29. Immortal Grapple: Only useful if opponent plays strike cards
: or weapons. The press it grants at superior is the only thing that saves
: it from being on the above list (and it's not like anyone plays this for
: the press at superior).

I'm not quite sure how this makes an almost-wallpaper list. As you
mentioned, S:CE is a very powerful effect, and widely available, which
makes things like Immortal Grapple (which prevents S:CE) very handy
if you want to play a combat deck (and win).

: 33. Skin of Steel: The Skin of Steel/Pulled Fangs combo is the

: only thing (in the original set) that prevents this card's usefulness from
: being entirely dependent on what one's opponent plays. Otherwise, it is
: an expensive and pointless way to prevent normal cardless hand slaps
: (since you lose a blood anyway, and can't play it if you don't have a
: blood).

What about Blur? Or any large Potence strike for that matter? Potence
combat did not suck in the basic set, and Skin of Steel is by far the
best fortitude card against big strikes. If the point you're getting
at is that things like SoS and Immortal Grapple rely on knowing that
people are likely to be playing S:CE or potence combat, you're right,
but I don't see how it matters. In order to design a deck at all, you
have to make some assumptions about what people will play. Generally
you make these guesses based on what cards seem to be highly useful,
powerful, or widely used.

: > Well, for one thing because you'd be better off putting a Skin of Steel

: > or two in your deck,

: To which I gave an honorable mention: See above.

Yeah, but I think you're wrong to do so. Do people in your playgroup
actually not play Skin of Steel? Don't you have anyone that plays
serious combat?

: > but besides that, the idea of punishing someone

: > for playing Brujah (or Ventrue, or Malkavian) is a little repugnant from
: > the standpoint of 'it's just punishing him for showing up and playing
: > the game.'

: Since when is trying to win "repugnant"? And how are clan hosers any
: different from putting a Far Mastery in your deck when you are tired of
: being hosed by Renegade Garou? Or putting in alot of intercept because
: you expect alot of stealth? Or putting in alot of Immortal Grapples (or
: psyches) because you expect alot of Strike: Combat Ends?

These are strategy-based decisions (choices based on what the in-game
environment looks like in terms of the methods people use to win and
otherwise accomplish their goals). Attacking vampires based on their
clan is not directly strategy-related - there are any number of possible
strategies someone could be pursuing, for example, with Volker, the
Puppet Prince. Using a clan hoser against Volker is different from
using a Bum's Rush on him because it doesn't fit into what I consider
to be the basic framework of the game.

: You'll have to explain this more because I really don't understand this at

: all. How is punishing someone for what is in his crypt any different from
: punishing him for what is in his library?

You use library cards to punish someone for what's in their library.
You also use library cards to punish someone for what's in their crypt.
You can't use crypt cards to punish someone for anything at all. Clearly
the crypt is qualitatively different from the library.

: > : Please name seven

: > : cards, and explain how their absence would make Jyhad unplayable.
: >
: > I can do this. ;-) In a basic-set Jyhad-only environment: Bum's Rush,
: > Haven Uncovered, Psyche, Fast Reaction, Hidden Lurker, Immortal Grapple,
: > Blood Hunt.

: Not bad, though my intention was not a basic-set only environment.
: Ironically, however, cards like Immortal Grapple are no different in
: principle than the "Clan Hosers" (except for that extra press, which is
: not what we play it for).

In that its usefulness depends on the environment, yes. But it depends
on a completely different aspect of the environment (strategies of
combat and combat defense rather than the happenstance of particular
vampire clans).

: > and

: > also eliminate any way to get around Strike: Combat Ends.

: You forgot Drawing out the Beast, Mariel, and Weather Control, especially
: when combined with Dawn Operation and Skin of Night. Still, S:CE is the
: most overpowered effect of the original set. Good thing there was a hoser
: for it, yes?

None of these really 'get around' S:CE except maybe Weather Control
(in severe multiple) - one point of damage per combat is not really
the kind of thing that makes a combat deck effective.

: No. It would not make the game unplayable--as I think you would find if

: you experimented with playing without these cards. It would do severe
: damage to the potential variety, and, as you have said, make many a great
: many cards, even clans, very hard to play. It would be a very different
: game environment, primarily of voters and bleeders. Ventrue, Malks, and
: Toreador would rule. Nossies and Gangrel would suffer (except for Wynn).
: Rush Allies would become more popular, as would anti ally cards like
: Kindred Segregation and Far Mastery. Anti-vote and anti-bleed cards would
: become popular and essential. Anti-Ventrue, anti-Malk, and anti-Toreador
: hosers would become essential too. Good thing the designers put in those
: 7 cards you listed, otherwise we really would have needed them hosers
: wouldn't we?

It would be a very different game without the major strategy of rush
combat.

: > : Just for fun, I think I would like to construct a Nosferatu "Toreador

: > : Hoser" Deck, complete with lots of Tragic Love Affairs and Nosferatu
: > : Performance Arts. Then I will wait for a good opportunity to use it. If
: > : my opponent complains that it is "lame" or "unfair" then he just has no
: > : sense of humor, now does he?
: >
: > Well, it won't be very funny for him, will it? How much fun is it to
: > be screwed by random chance?

: That's how I often get screwed, and it is often how I screw others. Would
: have won the last tournament if I hadn't got my KRCG contested and been
: bled by Freaky bleed Gangrel with Fame that he got out in the first turn.
: I have a real difficult time with this notion of yours that some ways of
: getting screwed are somehow less legitimate than others. If someone takes
: a chance, guesses at the game environment, and puts a clan hoser in his
: deck, why should he not be able to benefit from it substantially if he

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 25 Feb 1998, T.W.Malisch wrote:
> I'm an old Jyhad player and am not familiar with the new rules pertaining
> to ag damage. I pose these questions:
>
> 1) How much ag does it take to burn a vamp?
> Yuri has 3 blood. Will 3 ag burn him? 4 ag?

4 ag, as opposed to 5 under the old rules.

> 2) Do you still subtract one from the ag damage?
> Yuri with 3 blood takes 2 ag... does he go to torpor with 1 or 2 blood?

You never subtracted anything from the ag damage per se, even under the
old rules. Under the old rules you *did* subtract 1 from the amount of
blood you burn healing damage. This is because the first point of ag
damage you take shocks the system so you cannot heal, and sends you
immediately into torpor for being unable to burn a blood to heal the
damage. Only additional points of ag damage beyond the first caused the
loss of blood. You were burned if an (additional) point of ag damage
required you to burn blood, and you had no more left to lose.

Thus it required 2 ag damage to burn a vampire with no blood. The first
shocks the system so it cannot heal and sends to torpor. The second
requires him to burn a blood he does not have, resulting in his
destruction.

This is no longer true in the new rules. Each point of ag damage results
in a loss of blood. 1 ag damage to a vampire with no blood will burn him.
Pulled fangs now burns vampires, making it horrendously powerful.

> 3) does environmental damage come before or after ag hand damage?

Environmental damage has no specific time to it. Like most damage, it is
usually dealt during the strike resolution phase, simultaneous with any
aggravated damage also dealt in that phase.

Environmental damage cannot be contrasted with ag damage, since
environmental damage can also be either aggravated or normal.

> 4) with DOtB and Dawn Operation, would a vamp with no blood be burned from
> the one ag?

With the new rules, I'm afraid so.

> 5) what is the webpage URL where I can find the new rules?

Ummm....someone? I think LSJ just posted it;

> **) One extra question... can two vamps in combat both play TB... if not,
> then does one take precedence over the other?

Yes, but only if the first vamp plays it at inferior (as if anyone would).

Acting vampire gets the opportunity to play it first. If the acting
vampire plays it at superior, the blocking vamp is forbidden from doing so
(because she cannot play *any* cards).

All of this kinda reminds me of the reason I got into CCGs in the first

job and spent all my leisure time drinking and shagging and painting
miniatures and playing wargames. And then along came Magic where you got

unpredictable in the way that real people are, no matter how hard you work

beginning, I've only just recently started being a "serious" Jyhad player,
